sentence: NHS talking therapies are free psychological treatments for anxiety and depression, such as CBT and counselling.
note: NHS: CBT and counselling on the NHS; 'free' - flagged for second pass.

sentence: In England people aged 18 or over can usually refer themselves, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
note: NHS: self-refer if you live in England and are 18 or over; no diagnosis needed.

sentence: Services are also called IAPT, short for Improving Access to Psychological Therapies.
note: Naming from search summary.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.
note: Crisis route, see final section.

sentence: NHS talking therapies services treat common problems such as anxiety and depression with evidence-based psychological treatments.
note: NHS page title and summary; flagged for second pass.

sentence: They were previously known as Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, or IAPT, services.
note: Search summary: also known as IAPT.

sentence: Treatments include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and counselling for depression.
note: NHS.

sentence: Formats include a self-help workbook with a therapist's support, an online course, one-to-one sessions in person, by phone or by video, and group sessions.
note: NHS formats listed in search summary.

sentence: CBT is based on the idea that thoughts, feelings, behaviour and physical sensations are connected, and it helps people notice and challenge unhelpful patterns.
note: Local NHS service pages.

sentence: It is an active, practical therapy that includes exercises and homework.
note: Local NHS service pages.

sentence: Counselling for depression is a type of counselling developed for people with depression.
note: Local NHS service page.

sentence: Services should offer a choice of in-person or remotely delivered therapy.
note: Search summary of NHS England page.

sentence: Talking therapies can also help with mental health problems that come with long-term physical conditions, such as diabetes, cancer or long-term pain.
note: Search summary.

sentence: The NHS says people can refer themselves directly, without a referral from a GP, or a GP can refer them.
note: NHS.

sentence: Eligibility is mainly about age and location: people aged 18 or over who live in England can self-refer, and some areas also accept 16 and 17 year olds.
note: NHS.

sentence: A diagnosed mental health condition is not needed.
note: NHS: you do not need a diagnosis.

sentence: Some local services ask people to be registered with a GP in their area, so the local service's own page has the details.
note: Search summary: caveat on local rules.

sentence: People are usually contacted for an initial assessment, often by phone or video.
note: Search summary.

sentence: The therapist then recommends a treatment based on the symptoms and how severe they are.
note: Search summary.

sentence: Most services begin with a referral check and then a phone assessment, and some arrange a follow-up appointment to complete it.
note: Local NHS service pages.

sentence: Waiting times vary by area, so the local service can say how long the wait is.
note: Local pages: waiting times vary.

sentence: The self-referral route covers talking therapies rather than medicine, so a GP is still the route for a medicine review or a referral to a psychiatrist.
note: Search summary: self-referral is for talking therapies, not medication.

sentence: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run separate systems, so this route describes England.
note: Search note; flagged for second pass.

sentence: Talking therapies are not an emergency service. For urgent help, the routes below are open at any time.
note: Assignment brief: every mental-health page carries the crisis route; trust pages (gmmh urgent-help) list NHS urgent mental health support alongside 999.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
note: Trust pages: if life is at risk, someone is in immediate danger or has harmed themselves, call 999 or go to A&E.

sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf.
note: NHS trust page: call NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support; 24/7; can call for yourself or someone else.

sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
note: Samaritans 116 123 free, 24 hours: returned in the urgent-help and NHS grief searches.
